hook: The nun who spent her life caring for the poorest of the poor in Calcutta.

pages.x: Anjezë Gonxhe Bojaxhiu was born in 1910 in Skopje to an Albanian family. Her father died when she was eight. At 18 she left home to become a nun with the Sisters of Loreto in Ireland, and never saw her mother again.
In 1929 she was sent to India, took the name Teresa, and for nearly 20 years taught at a girls' school in Calcutta.
On 10 September 1946, on a train to Darjeeling, she felt what she called "a call within a call": to leave the convent and live among the poorest of the poor.
In 1948 she put on a cheap white sari with blue borders and went to live in the slums. In 1950 she founded the Missionaries of Charity, a new order of nuns.
In 1952 she opened a home where the dying poor, picked up from the streets, could die in peace and with dignity. Homes for people with leprosy, for orphans, and later for people with AIDS followed.
In 1979 she won the Nobel Peace Prize. She asked for the grand dinner in her honour to be cancelled, and the money given to the poor.
Critics said her homes gave poor medical care, and that she took money from dictators. Letters published after her death in 1997 showed that for nearly 50 years she had felt that God was absent.
Mother Teresa became a worldwide symbol of care for the poorest. By her death her order ran more than 600 missions in over 120 countries. The Catholic Church made her a saint in 2016.
